2.s: What is the Earth's spinning on its axis called?
2.x: Rotation – The Earth spinning on its axis (line through both poles); revolution = moving round the Sun

2.x: Angular speed – 15° per hour (1° in 4 min)

2.s: What is the linear speed of the Earth's rotation at the poles?

2.s: Why do we not feel the Earth's rotation?

2.s: Why does the Pole Star seem fixed in the sky?

It does not move in space
2.x: Pole Star – Seems fixed – it lies almost in line with the Earth's axis of rotation; it marks north, so walking east it is on your left

2.s: What is a sidereal day measured against?
2.x: Sidereal (one true rotation) – A distant star – 23 h 56 min 4.09 s

2.s: How long is a sidereal day?
2.x: Sidereal (one true rotation) – A distant star – 23 h 56 min 4.09 s

2.s: What is a solar day measured against?
2.x: Solar – The Sun – 24 h (~4 min longer, as the Earth also moves along its orbit)

2.s: Why is a solar day about 4 minutes longer than a sidereal day?

The Moon pulls the Earth back
2.x: Solar – The Sun – 24 h (~4 min longer, as the Earth also moves along its orbit)

2.s: Which rhythm do day and night produce?

2.x: Day and night – The diurnal rhythm of daylight and air temperature

2.s: What does Coriolis deflection do to moving air and water?
2.x: Coriolis deflection – Flow paths of air and water turned sideways

2.s: Why does a place get high tides twice a day?

Rotation carries it through the two tidal bulges
2.x: Movement of the tides – A place is carried through the tidal bulges twice a day

2.s: Which of these is an effect of the Earth's rotation?
2.x: Also – Time difference between longitudes, centrifugal bulge

2.s: What causes day and night on Earth?
2.x: Seasons – Caused by revolution + tilt (not rotation); day and night come from rotation, not revolution

2.s: What would happen if the Earth stopped rotating?

2.x: No rotation – No sunrise / sunset and no day-night cycle; seasons would remain

2.s: What would happen to gravity at the Equator if the Earth rotated faster?
2.x: Faster rotation – Stronger centrifugal effect → g decreases at the Equator, unchanged at the poles

2.s: Which 5th-century Indian astronomer first explained that the Earth's rotation causes sunrise and sunset?
2.x: Aryabhata (5th century) – First explained that the rotation of the Earth causes the daily rising and setting of the Sun (*Aryabhatiya*; also *Aryasiddhanta*)

2.s: What did the Foucault pendulum (Paris, 1851) show to prove the Earth rotates?

It points to the Pole Star
2.x: Foucault pendulum, Paris 1851 – The plane of swing slowly turns

2.s: Which of these is a proof of Earth's rotation?
2.x: Other proofs – Coriolis deflection, equatorial bulge, apparent east-to-west motion of the sky

2.s: How much has polar ice melt lengthened the day, per 2024 studies?
2.x: Studies (ETH Zurich, *Nature Geoscience* / *PNAS* 2024) show the rotation axis drifting and the day lengthening; cause = mass redistribution: as polar ice melts, water moves towards the Equator (also groundwater loss) – day longer by ~1.33 ms per century (2000–2020).

2.s: Which of these bombards the upper atmosphere with energy but does not shift the Earth's axis?
2.x: Solar flares and CMEs bombard the upper atmosphere with energy but do not shift the axis.

2.s: What causes the Coriolis force?
2.x: Coriolis force – An apparent force caused by the Earth's rotation; shapes winds, ocean currents, cyclones and large-scale weather patterns

2.s: Which law says moving air is deflected right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern?
2.x: Ferrel's law – Moving air and water are deflected to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere

2.s: Where is the Coriolis force zero?
2.x: Force = 2Ωv sin(latitude) – Zero at the Equator, maximum at the poles; grows with latitude and wind speed; linked to the decreasing rotational velocity with increasing latitude

2.s: How close to the Equator do cyclones rarely form?
2.x: Cyclones – Rarely form within 5° of the Equator; NH cyclones spin anticlockwise, SH clockwise

2.x: Cyclone Montha (Oct 2025) – Steered north-northwest to the Kakinada coast

2.s: Which force of rotation causes the equatorial bulge and polar flattening?

2.s: Besides the Moon's and Sun's pull, what causes the tidal bulge on the far side of the Earth?

2.s: What force is subtracted from gravitational attraction to give the tide-generating force?
2.x: Tide-generating force – Gravitational attraction − centrifugal force

2.s: How far apart are successive high tides in a semi-diurnal tide?

2.s: What is the position of Sun, Earth and Moon during a spring tide?

2.s: When do neap tides occur?
o: At new moon and full moon
2.x: Neap (lowest range) – Sun and Moon at right angles – First and third quarter, ~7 days after spring tides – twice a month

2.s: When do the highest spring tides occur?

When the Moon is at perigee

2.s: What is a falling tide called?
2.x: Ebb / flow (flood) – Falling tide / rising tide

2.s: Where is the difference between day and night lengths least?
2.x: Unequal day and night – Tilt + revolution; difference least near the Equator (~12 h day all year), increasing away from it to the poles

2.s: How long do day and night each last at the poles?
2.x: Poles – ~6 months of day + 6 months of night (revolution with axial tilt)

2.s: Where is twilight shortest?

2.s: What marks the seasons near the Equator, rather than day length?
2.x: Equatorial seasons – Marked by wet and dry periods, not by day length

2.x: Orbit – Slightly elliptical, Sun at one focus

2.s: How long does the Earth take for one revolution of the Sun?
2.x: Period – ~365¼ days (365.25; sidereal year 365 d 6 h 9 min 9.5 s)

2.x: Mean speed – 29.78 km/s; the Sun's gravity is the centripetal force

2.x: Aphelion – Early July (~152 million km; 6 July in 2026); the Earth–Sun distance is not constant

2.x: Seasons – Revolution + 23½° tilt + parallelism of the axis

2.x: Circular orbit instead of elliptical – The varying distance would vanish, so the difference between seasons would be reduced – a small effect, since tilt is the main cause

2.x: Leap year – Extra ¼ day a year → 366 days (29 February); a century year only if divisible by 400 (2000 yes, 1900 no)

2.x: Revolution – Year, seasons, solstices, equinoxes, perihelion / aphelion

5.x: Role – Broken into plates – Plates glide over it; main source of magma

5.s: Which layer do plates glide over, and is the main source of magma?
5.x: Role – Broken into plates – Plates glide over it; main source of magma

5.s: What is the core called in the sequence lithosphere → asthenosphere → mesosphere → ?
5.x: Sequence: lithosphere → asthenosphere → mesosphere → barysphere (core).

5.s: What depth is the dense lower layer of the Indian plate under Tibet delaminating at?

5.s: Which are the IUGG mantle zones?

5.s: Which is the most important indirect source of information about the Earth's interior?
o: Rise of temperature and pressure with depth
5.x: Surface rocks from mining areas and deep drilling – Seismic waves – most important

5.s: Which indirect source of information on the Earth's interior arrives from space as solid material?
5.x: Kola Peninsula (USSR, 1970s): ~12 km, deepest hole – Meteorites

5.s: What kind of sources of knowledge about the Earth's interior are seismic data and meteorites?
5.x: Seismic, gravity and magnetic data and meteorites are indirect sources.

6.s: How are igneous rocks formed?
o: By heat and pressure on rocks
By cooling and solidification of magma or lava

6.s: Which rocks are known as primary rocks?

6.s: Which feature belongs to igneous rocks?
6.x: Features – No layers, no fossils; both crystalline and non-crystalline

6.s: Why does granite have no fossils?
6.x: Granite – Igneous, has no fossils – formed from magma

6.s: Which of these is NOT an igneous rock?
6.x: Not igneous – Quartzite (metamorphic), dolomite

6.s: Why do intrusive (plutonic) rocks have large crystals?
o: They cool fast at the surface
6.x: Intrusive (plutonic) – Cools slowly at depth → large grains / crystals – Granite, gabbro, diorite, pegmatite

6.s: Which of these are intrusive (plutonic) igneous rocks?
6.x: Intrusive (plutonic) – Cools slowly at depth → large grains / crystals – Granite, gabbro, diorite, pegmatite

6.s: Why do extrusive (volcanic) rocks have fine grains?
o: Lava cools fast at the surface
6.x: Extrusive (volcanic) – Lava cools fast at the surface → fine grains – Basalt, rhyolite, andesite

6.s: Which of these are extrusive (volcanic) igneous rocks?
6.x: Extrusive (volcanic) – Lava cools fast at the surface → fine grains – Basalt, rhyolite, andesite

6.s: To which silica class does rhyolite belong?

6.s: To which silica class does granite belong?
6.x: Granite – Felsic intrusive

6.s: To which silica class does basalt belong?
6.x: Basalt – Mafic extrusive

6.s: What are silica-rich, light-coloured igneous rocks rich in quartz and feldspar called?

6.s: Which minerals are mafic and dark in colour?
6.x: Felsic: silica-rich, light-coloured, rich in quartz and feldspar, poor in Fe, Mg, Ca. Mafic (basic): rich in Fe, Mg, Ca; dark, dense – olivine and pyroxene are mafic minerals and dark in colour.

6.s: Which rock mainly makes up the Deccan Traps?
6.x: Rock – The Deccan Plateau / Deccan Traps are made mainly of basalt – igneous lava flows

6.s: When were the Deccan Traps formed by fissure eruptions?
6.x: Origin – Fissure eruptions at the end of the Cretaceous, ~65–66 million years ago, as India passed over the Réunion hotspot

6.s: What share of the Earth's crust by weight is oxygen?
6.x: 1 – Oxygen – 46.6 – most abundant element (in oxides and silicates)

6.s: Which is the second most abundant element in the Earth's crust?
6.x: 2 – Silicon – 27.7 – second; not a metal; bulk of rocks and minerals as silica/silicates

6.s: Which is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust?
6.x: 3 – Aluminium – 8.1 – most abundant metal

6.s: What share of the Earth's crust by weight is aluminium?
6.x: 3 – Aluminium – 8.1 – most abundant metal

6.s: Which is the second most abundant metal in the Earth's crust?
6.x: 4 – Iron – 5.0 – second-most abundant metal

6.s: What share of the Earth's crust by weight is iron?
6.x: 4 – Iron – 5.0 – second-most abundant metal

6.s: Which elements rank 5th to 8th in the Earth's crust by weight?
6.x: 5–8 – Calcium, sodium, potassium, magnesium – 3.6, 2.8, 2.6, 2.1

6.s: What share of the Earth's crust by weight is calcium?
6.x: 5–8 – Calcium, sodium, potassium, magnesium – 3.6, 2.8, 2.6, 2.1

6.s: Which of these elements is the least abundant in the Earth's crust?
6.x: Highest and lowest among O, Si, Ca, Na, Mg: oxygen and magnesium. The element present in large amounts in rocks and minerals is silicon.

6.s: What share of the Earth's crust is made of feldspar?
6.x: Feldspar – Si and O common to all feldspars; Na, K, Ca, Al in specific varieties; makes up about one-half of the crust

6.s: Which mineral: SiO₂ (silicon dioxide); hard, resists weathering; Mohs 7; major part of granite and sandstone?
6.x: Quartz – SiO₂ (silicon dioxide); hard, resists weathering; Mohs 7; major part of granite and sandstone

6.s: Which of these is NOT a form of calcium carbonate?
6.x: Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) – Limestone, chalk and marble (granite is not a form of CaCO₃)

6.s: Which mineral is a single-chain inosilicate (pyroxene)?
6.x: Inosilicate – single chain – Augite (pyroxene)

6.s: Which mineral is a double-chain inosilicate (amphibole)?
6.x: Inosilicate – double chain – Hornblende (amphibole)

6.s: Which minerals are sheet silicates (phyllosilicates)?
6.x: Phyllosilicate (sheet) – Muscovite, biotite (mica)

6.s: Which minerals are framework silicates (tectosilicates)?
6.x: Tectosilicate (framework) – Albite, orthoclase (feldspar), quartz

6.s: What is the order in which minerals crystallise from magma called?
6.x: Bowen's reaction series = order in which minerals crystallise from magma: olivine first → pyroxene → amphibole → biotite → K-feldspar → muscovite → quartz last (most stable).

6.s: Which scale measures the hardness of minerals?
6.x: Mohs scale measures hardness of minerals: talc 1, gypsum 2, calcite 3, fluorite 4, apatite 5, orthoclase 6, quartz 7, topaz 8, corundum 9, diamond 10. (Mercalli/Rossi-Forel = earthquake intensity; Beaufort = wind.)

6.s: Which mineral (SiO₂, Mohs 7) is a major part of granite and sandstone?
6.x: Quartz – SiO₂ (silicon dioxide); hard, resists weathering; Mohs 7; major part of granite and sandstone

6.s: Which mineral crystallises first from magma in Bowen's reaction series?
6.x: Bowen's reaction series – Order in which minerals crystallise from magma: olivine first → pyroxene → amphibole → biotite → K-feldspar → muscovite → quartz last (most stable)

6.s: Which mineral has hardness 8 on the Mohs scale?
6.x: Mohs scale – Hardness of minerals: talc 1, gypsum 2, calcite 3, fluorite 4, apatite 5, orthoclase 6, quartz 7, topaz 8, corundum 9, diamond 10

6.s: What does the Mercalli scale measure?
6.x: Other scales – Mercalli/Rossi-Forel = earthquake intensity; Beaufort = wind

6.s: By which system at the Earth's surface are sedimentary rocks formed?
6.x: Formation – At the Earth's surface by the hydrological system, from weathering of pre-existing rocks; sediments transported, deposited, compacted and lithified in layers (strata) → "stratified rocks"

6.s: Which resources do sedimentary rocks hold?
6.x: Fossils and resources – Contain fossils; hold most fossils and coal, petroleum, natural gas

6.s: What share of the Earth's surface is covered by sedimentary rocks?
6.x: Extent – About 75% of the Earth's surface

6.s: Of which rock are the Red Fort and Agra Fort built?
6.x: Sandstone – Forms under water; the Red Fort and Agra Fort are built of red sandstone

6.s: What type of rocks mainly make up the Himalayas?
6.x: Himalayan rocks – Mainly sedimentary (folded Tethys sediments)

6.s: In which colours does limestone occur?
6.x: Limestone – Occurs white as well as black

6.s: Which of these are mechanically formed (clastic) sedimentary rocks?
6.x: Mechanically (clastic) – Sandstone, conglomerate, shale, loess

6.s: Which of these are chemically formed sedimentary rocks?
6.x: Chemically – Rock salt, gypsum, halite, chert, limestone

6.s: Which of these are organically formed sedimentary rocks?
6.x: Organically – Coal (Uttarakhand 2006), chalk, coral limestone

6.s: Which rock is both porous and very permeable, making good aquifers?
6.x: Porous and permeable – Chalk (very permeable, aquifers), sandstone

6.s: Which rock is porous but impermeable?
6.x: Porous but impermeable – Clay – very fine pores, poorly connected

6.s: Which rock is neither porous nor permeable?
6.x: Neither – Granite

6.s: What are fossils?
o: Preserved remains or traces of ancient organisms
6.x: Fossils – Preserved remains, impressions or traces of ancient organisms

6.s: Which method is used to find the age of the Earth?
6.x: Age of the Earth – Uranium (radiometric) dating; carbon dating only for young organic remains

6.s: Who made the first geological time scale in 1760?
6.x: First geological time scale – Giovanni Arduino (1760)

6.s: Which era of the Phanerozoic lasted from about 550 to 250 million years ago?
6.x: Geological eras (Phanerozoic) – Paleozoic ~550–250 mya → Mesozoic 250–66 mya → Cenozoic (66 mya – present)

6.s: When did the dinosaurs die out?
6.x: Dinosaurs: Mesozoic era – Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous; died out ~66 million years ago

6.s: Which period did the Paleogene (65-23 mya) follow?
6.x: Paleogene Period (65-23 mya) – Followed the Cretaceous

6.s: Which eruptions in India, along with a meteor impact, are linked to the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction?
6.x: Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction – Fifth Extinction, 66 mya; Deccan Traps eruptions and a meteor impact – Chicxulub Crater (Yucatan, Mexico)

6.s: What turns igneous or sedimentary rocks into metamorphic rocks?
6.x: Igneous or sedimentary rocks recrystallise under heat and pressure ("change of form") – metamorphic rocks come from both.

6.s: Which metamorphic rock forms from limestone?
6.x: Limestone (and chalk, dolomite) – Marble

6.s: Which metamorphic rock forms from shale or clay?
6.x: Shale / clay – Slate (then schist)

6.s: Which metamorphic rock forms from sandstone?
6.x: Sandstone – Quartzite

6.s: Which metamorphic rock forms from granite?
6.x: Granite – Gneiss

6.s: Which metamorphic rocks form from basalt?
6.x: Basalt – Amphibolite, schist

6.s: What does coal turn into by metamorphism, via anthracite?
6.x: Coal – Graphite (via anthracite)

6.s: Which of these is NOT a typical metamorphic mineral?
6.x: Typical metamorphic minerals – Garnet, kyanite, sillimanite, staurolite (halite is not one)

6.s: Which group consists only of metamorphic rocks?
6.x: Metamorphic – Gneiss, marble, quartzite, slate

6.s: Which group consists only of sedimentary rocks?
6.x: Sedimentary – Sandstone, limestone, shale

6.s: Which of these is an igneous rock?
6.x: Igneous – Granite

6.s: What is the last stage of the metamorphic series coal → anthracite → ?
6.x: Coal and diamond – Both are carbon – diamond forms from carbon under extreme pressure; the metamorphic series is coal → anthracite → graphite

6.s: What is the science of rocks, a branch of geology, called?
6.x: Petrology – Science (study) of rocks, a branch of geology; rocks: igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic

6.s: Which process turns deposited sediments into sedimentary rock in the rock cycle?
6.x: Rock cycle – Magma → (cooling) igneous → (weathering, erosion, deposition, lithification) sedimentary → (heat, pressure) metamorphic → (melting) magma

6.s: What does lithology describe?
o: The physical character of a rock unit
6.x: Lithology – Physical character of a rock unit – texture, grain size, composition

6.s: How does enhanced rock weathering lock up CO₂?
o: Crushed basalt spread on farmland locks it as bicarbonate
6.x: Enhanced rock weathering – Crushed basalt spread on farmland locks CO₂ as bicarbonate

6.s: What does exposed metamorphic rock weather into in the rock cycle?
6.x: Any rock type can become another; exposed metamorphic rock weathers into sediment.

6.s: Which acid, formed by rainwater with dissolved CO₂, weathers rocks?
6.x: Rainwater with dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid, which weathers rocks.

7.s: Who proposed the theory of continental drift in 1912?
7.x: Continental drift – Alfred Wegener (German), 1912

7.s: Why was Wegener's theory of continental drift rejected?
o: The drift forces he proposed were too weak
7.x: Drift forces – Pole-fleeing force (Earth's rotation) and tidal force (Sun and Moon) – too weak, so the theory was rejected

7.s: What was the original supercontinent in Wegener's theory called?
7.x: Original landmass – Pangaea, surrounded by the mega-ocean Panthalassa

7.s: What was the northern part of Pangaea called?
7.x: Split – Into Laurasia (north) and Gondwanaland (south), separated by the Tethys Sea

7.s: When did Pangaea begin to split, according to Wegener's theory?
7.x: Date of split – Began about 200 million years ago; older books round Pangaea's break-up to ~225 million years (also given for Gondwanaland's break-up)

7.s: How many million years ago did Gondwanaland break up, according to some textbooks?
7.x: Other dates – "Pangaea split 150 million years ago" and "Gondwanaland broke up 65 million years ago" also appear; dates differ between textbooks

7.s: Which present landmasses formed Laurasia?
o: North America, Greenland, Europe, Asia (minus India)
7.x: Laurasia – North America, Greenland, Europe, Asia (minus India)

7.s: Who: South America, Africa, India, Australia, Antarctica, Madagascar, Arabia?
7.x: Gondwanaland – South America, Africa, India, Australia, Antarctica, Madagascar, Arabia

7.s: Which landmass was part of Gondwanaland, not Laurasia?
7.x: India (Peninsular) was part of Gondwanaland, not Laurasia; North America was not part of Gondwanaland.

7.s: Which two continents show the jig-saw fit, confirmed by Bullard's 1964 computer fit?
7.x: Jig-saw fit – South America and Africa; Bullard's 1964 computer fit

7.s: Which region matches the ~2,000-million-year rock belt of the Brazil coast?
7.x: Rock belts – ~2,000-million-year belt of the Brazil coast matches West Africa

7.s: Which gold placer deposits have their source in gold-bearing veins in Brazil?
7.x: Placer deposits – Ghana coast gold has no local source; its source is the gold-bearing veins in Brazil – the continents lay side by side

7.s: Which glacial sediments (tillite) of India have counterparts in six southern landmasses?
7.x: Tillite – Gondwana glacial sediments of India have counterparts in six southern landmasses

7.s: Which fossil reptile found only in South Africa and Brazil supports continental drift?
7.x: Fossils – Mesosaurus (South Africa and Brazil only); Glossopteris; lemurs

7.s: On which semi-fluid layer do the rigid lithospheric plates move?
7.x: Plate tectonics – Pieces of the Earth's crust (lithospheric plates) are in constant slow motion driven by movement in the mantle – rigid lithosphere on the semi-fluid asthenosphere

7.s: Who proposed the theory of plate tectonics in 1967?
7.x: Authors – 1967 by McKenzie and Parker, and independently by Morgan

7.s: On which concept is the plate tectonics theory based?
7.x: Basis – Based on sea-floor spreading

7.s: Which theory did H.H. Hess give in 1960–62?
7.x: H.H. Hess – Gave sea-floor spreading (1960–62), not plate tectonics

7.s: How is plate movement tracked today?
7.x: Monitoring – Plate movement is tracked with GPS data

7.s: In which year did Wegener propose continental drift?
7.x: 1912 – Wegener – continental drift

7.s: In which year: Arthur Holmes – convection currents; heat from radioactive decay?
7.x: 1930s – Arthur Holmes – convection currents; heat from radioactive decay

7.s: In which years did Hess put forward sea-floor spreading?
7.x: 1960–62 – Hess – sea-floor spreading

7.s: Whose 1963 work on magnetic bands supported sea-floor spreading?
7.x: 1963 – Vine–Matthews

7.s: In which year: Plate tectonics?
7.x: 1967 – Plate tectonics

7.s: Which of these is one of the seven major plates?
7.x: Seven major plates: Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian, Antarctic.

7.s: Where is Cocos?
o: Between the Asiatic and Pacific plates
Between the Philippine and Indian plates
Between Central America and the Pacific plate
7.x: Cocos – Between Central America and the Pacific plate

7.s: Where is Nazca?
o: Between the Philippine and Indian plates
Between South America and the Pacific plate
Between the Asiatic and Pacific plates
7.x: Nazca – Between South America and the Pacific plate

7.s: Which minor plate lies between the Philippine and Indian plates?
7.x: Caroline – Between the Philippine and Indian plates

7.s: Which minor plate lies between the Asiatic and Pacific plates?
7.x: Philippine – Between the Asiatic and Pacific plates

7.s: Which minor plate is made up mostly of the Saudi landmass?
7.x: Arabian – Mostly the Saudi Arabian landmass

7.s: What does palaeomagnetic data show about the Indian landmass?
o: It moved northward from south of the equator
7.x: Palaeomagnetic data – The Indian landmass has moved northward from south of the equator

7.s: Which period was the Indian Peninsula joined to Africa until?
7.x: Link with Africa – The Peninsula was joined to Africa until the Cretaceous

7.s: Over which hotspot did India pass when the Deccan Traps erupted?
7.x: Deccan Traps – Erupted as India crossed near the equator over the Réunion hotspot

7.s: When did India's collision with Eurasia begin?
7.x: Collision with Eurasia – Began ~40–50 million years ago (4–5 crore); the Tethys closed and its sediments were folded into the Himalayas

7.s: What rate does the Indian Plate still move north at?
7.x: Present motion – India still moves north ~5 cm/year → the Himalayas are still rising (~5 mm/year)

7.s: What causes earthquakes from the Himalayas to the Arakan Yoma?
o: Collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates
7.x: Earthquakes – From the Himalayas to the Arakan Yoma and in the north-west: caused by the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates (plate tectonics, not volcanoes, corals or dams)

7.s: What landforms resulted from the Indian Plate's collision with Eurasia?
o: The Himalayas and the Indo-Gangetic foreland basin
7.x: Results – The Himalayas and the Indo-Gangetic foreland basin

7.s: What is happening to the Indian plate's lower layer under southern Tibet?
o: It is melting at the surface
It is rising into the crust
7.x: Under southern Tibet – Delamination of the plate's lower layer at ~100 km

7.s: What happens at mid-ocean ridges according to sea-floor spreading?
7.x: Sea-floor spreading – Harry Hess, 1960–62: magma rises at mid-ocean ridges → new crust is continually added

7.s: Which process destroys old oceanic crust?
7.x: Balance – Old crust is destroyed by subduction – the two roughly balance

7.s: What increases in oceanic crust away from the mid-ocean ridge?
7.x: Away from the ridge – The age, density and thickness of oceanic crust and its sediments increase

7.s: How old are the oldest rocks of the ocean floor?
7.x: Age of ocean floor – Rocks are young; the oldest are ~200 million years

7.s: What does palaeomagnetism show about rocks?
o: They are all the same age
They record the magnetic field of their time
7.x: Palaeomagnetism – Rocks record the field of their time

7.s: How do normal and reversed magnetic bands lie on either side of a mid-ocean ridge?
7.x: Vine and Matthews (1963) – Normal and reversed bands lie symmetrically on either side of the ridge

7.s: How much did the seafloor sink in one observed burst of sea-floor spreading?
7.x: Bursts – One observed episode – seafloor sank 4 m, spread over 1 m, 160 million m³ of lava in 16 days

7.s: How often has the Earth's magnetic field reversed?
7.x: The Earth's magnetic field has reversed every few hundred thousand years; the early atmosphere had no 54% oxygen; living organisms modified the early atmosphere.

7.s: How do plates move at a divergent (constructive) boundary?
7.x: Divergent (constructive) – Apart; new crust – Mid-Atlantic Ridge; Red Sea, East African Rift (Nubian, Somalian, Arabian plates near the Afar triple junction)

7.s: How do plates move at a convergent (destructive) boundary?
7.x: Convergent (destructive) – Collision / subduction; mountains, trenches; no new crust – Himalayas (continent–continent); Andes (Nazca under South American); Mariana Trench (ocean–ocean)

7.s: Which mountains formed where the Nazca plate subducts under the South American plate?
7.x: Convergent (destructive) – Collision / subduction; mountains, trenches; no new crust – Himalayas (continent–continent); Andes (Nazca under South American); Mariana Trench (ocean–ocean)

7.s: How do plates move at a transform (conservative) boundary?
7.x: Transform (conservative) – Slide past – San Andreas; Sagaing Fault (Myanmar, Indian–Eurasian)

7.s: Which are examples of transform plate boundaries?
o: Mid-Atlantic Ridge and East African Rift
7.x: Transform (conservative) – Slide past – San Andreas; Sagaing Fault (Myanmar, Indian–Eurasian)

7.s: What causes earthquakes at convergent plate boundaries?
7.x: Convergent earthquakes – From subduction friction (Ring of Fire)

7.s: Which mountains are examples of cordilleran (continent–ocean) convergence?
7.x: Cordilleran convergence – Another name for continent–ocean (C-O) convergence – builds extensive fold mountains close to the coast, e.g. the Rockies and the Andes (cordillera = an extensive mountain chain)

7.s: Which two plates does the Owen Fracture Zone separate?
7.x: Owen Fracture Zone – Separates the Arabian and Indian plates

7.s: What formed the Ladakh Magmatic Arc?
o: Northward subduction of the Neo-Tethys plate
7.x: Ladakh Magmatic Arc – Northward subduction of the Neo-Tethys plate

7.s: Which plates did the Pacific-Farallon Plate subduct beneath to form the Isthmus of Panama?
7.x: Isthmus of Panama – Subduction of the Pacific-Farallon Plate beneath the Caribbean and South American plates → volcanic arc

7.s: What do sudden earth movements cause?
7.x: Sudden movements – Earthquakes and volcanoes

7.s: What do slow (diastrophic) earth movements build?
7.x: Slow (diastrophic) movements – Build continents and mountains

8.s: What does the magnitude of an earthquake measure?
8.x: Measures – Energy released at the focus (from the amplitude of seismic waves) – Degree of shaking and damage observed at a place

8.s: What does the intensity of an earthquake measure?
o: Degree of shaking and damage at a place
8.x: Measures – Energy released at the focus (from the amplitude of seismic waves) – Degree of shaking and damage observed at a place

8.s: What kind of measure is earthquake magnitude?
8.x: Nature – Quantitative; one value per earthquake – Qualitative; varies from place to place, falls with distance from the epicentre

8.s: How does earthquake intensity behave across places?
o: It varies from place to place, falling with distance from the epicentre
8.x: Nature – Quantitative; one value per earthquake – Qualitative; varies from place to place, falls with distance from the epicentre

8.s: In which year did Charles F. Richter devise the Richter scale?
8.x: Scale – Richter (Charles F. Richter, 1935); now Moment Magnitude (Mw) – Modified Mercalli (MMI), MSK-64, old Rossi-Forel – all I to XII

8.s: Which of these is an earthquake intensity scale?
8.x: Scale – Richter (Charles F. Richter, 1935); now Moment Magnitude (Mw) – Modified Mercalli (MMI), MSK-64, old Rossi-Forel – all I to XII

8.s: How much does energy rise with each whole number on the Richter scale?
8.x: Richter scale – Logarithmic, based on the amplitude of seismic waves; each whole number = 10× amplitude and about 31–32× energy (two steps ≈ 1,000×)

8.s: What is the moment magnitude (Mw) scale based on?
o: Rupture area of the fault and size of the waves
8.x: Moment magnitude (Mw) – Based on the rupture area of the fault and the size of the waves; preferred for large quakes (Richter works best for regional quakes up to ~M5)

8.s: What does the Mercalli scale measure?
8.x: Mercalli scale – Measures earthquakes (intensity, from observed effects) – not cyclones, floods or tornadoes

8.s: In which year was the MSK-64 intensity scale recommended at a UNESCO meeting?
8.x: MSK-64 (Medvedev–Sponheuer–Karnik) – Intensity scale recommended in 1964 at the UNESCO intergovernmental meeting; used in India (BIS zones are defined in MSK)

8.s: What is Mercator, which is not a seismic scale?
8.x: Mercator – A map projection, not a seismic scale

8.s: Which scale measures earthquake intensity, while Richter measures magnitude?
8.x: Richter measures magnitude and Mercalli measures intensity; in loose usage the Richter scale is also called the scale of earthquake intensity.

8.s: What is the effect of an earthquake below magnitude 3.0?
o: Recorded but rarely felt, no damage
8.x: below 3.0 – Micro/minor – recorded, rarely felt, no damage

8.s: What is the effect of an earthquake of magnitude 3.0–3.9?
8.x: 3.0–3.9 – Often felt, very rarely damage

8.s: What is an earthquake of magnitude 4.0–4.9 called?
8.x: 4.0–4.9 – Light – felt by most, none to minimal damage

8.s: What does a moderate earthquake (5.0–5.9) do?
8.x: 5.0–5.9 – Moderate – damages poorly built houses

8.s: In which magnitude class was the Latur earthquake of 1993?
In which magnitude class was the Bhuj earthquake of 2001 (Mw 7.7)?
Which earthquake was a great earthquake of magnitude 9.5?
8.x: 8.0 + – Great (Assam–Tibet 1950 8.6; Chile 1960 9.5)

8.s: What does a seismograph do?
8.x: Seismograph – Detects and records seismic waves; its readings give magnitude (books also call it the device for intensity)

8.s: What is a seismometer?
8.x: Seismometer – The sensor (pendulum / spring mass) inside a seismograph

8.s: What is a seismogram?
8.x: Seismogram – The recording itself

8.s: Which instrument only shows that a tremor occurred and its time?
8.x: Seismoscope – Only shows that a tremor occurred and its time

8.s: Which instrument records slow slip along a fault?
8.x: Tiltmeter / Creepmeter – Ground tilt / slow slip (creep) along a fault

11.s: What sets weathering apart from erosion?
11.x: Weathering – Natural breaking down and decay of rocks in situ (at or near the surface) into fragments, clays and dissolved matter; no transport is involved

11.s: What does erosion do?
11.x: Erosion – Carries the loosened material away

11.s: What are weathering, mass wasting, erosion and deposition together called?
11.x: Geomorphic processes – Shape the Earth's surface – weathering, mass wasting, erosion, deposition (endogenic forces build relief, exogenic forces wear it down)

11.s: Which of these is a physical (mechanical) weathering process?
11.x: Physical (mechanical) – Exfoliation, frost wedging (freeze-thaw), salt-crystal growth, block disintegration – Breaks rock without chemical change; driven mainly by temperature variation – typical of hot deserts and cold mountains

11.s: Which chemical weathering process dissolves soluble minerals such as rock salt and gypsum?
11.x: Chemical – Solution – Soluble minerals (rock salt, gypsum) dissolve

11.s: What happens in solution weathering?
o: Soluble minerals like rock salt dissolve
11.x: Chemical – Solution – Soluble minerals (rock salt, gypsum) dissolve

11.s: Which chemical weathering process is rainwater with dissolved CO₂ (carbonic acid) attacking limestone?
11.x: Chemical – Carbonation – CO₂ in rain forms carbonic acid, dissolves limestone (karst) and stores carbon as bicarbonate

11.s: Which chemical weathering process makes iron minerals rust, giving red/yellow soils?
11.x: Chemical – Oxidation – Oxygen dissolved in water reacts with iron minerals – rusting → red/yellow soils

11.s: What does oxidation of iron minerals give rise to in soils?
11.x: Chemical – Oxidation – Oxygen dissolved in water reacts with iron minerals – rusting → red/yellow soils

11.s: Which chemical weathering process makes minerals absorb water and swell (anhydrite → gypsum)?
11.x: Chemical – Hydration – Minerals absorb water and swell: anhydrite → gypsum

11.x: Chemical – Hydration – Minerals absorb water and swell: anhydrite → gypsum

11.s: Which chemical weathering process changes muscovite into vermiculite as potassium is replaced by hydronium?

11.s: What replaces interlayer potassium when muscovite turns into vermiculite?
11.x: Chemical – Hydrolysis – Water (H⁺/hydronium) reacts with silicates: feldspar → clay; muscovite → vermiculite when interlayer potassium is replaced by hydronium

11.s: What drives biological weathering?

11.s: In which climate is chemical weathering fastest?
11.x: Climate control – Chemical weathering is fastest in hot and humid (wet) climates – heat and abundant water speed up reactions (tropics); slowest in cold or dry climates

11.s: Which gas held in rainwater forms carbonic acid that weathers rocks?
11.x: Rain as an agent – Rainwater holds CO₂ in solution (→ carbonic acid, carbonation) and atmospheric oxygen (→ oxidation) – both explain why rainfall weathers rocks

11.s: What mainly causes mechanical weathering?
11.x: Mechanical weathering – Mainly caused by temperature variation; this does not explain the definition of weathering as in-situ decay

11.s: Which of these is a physical weathering process, unlike hydration and oxidation?

11.s: Of which process is oxidation a part?
11.x: Oxidation – A weathering process, not mass wasting

11.s: Which weathering process changes muscovite into vermiculite?

17.x: Convection – Vertical transfer – warm air rises, cool air sinks (troposphere)

17.s: Which process transfers heat horizontally by wind, as with the Loo?
17.x: Advection – Horizontal transfer by wind (e.g. the Loo)

17.x: Terrestrial radiation – Long-wave infra-red from the Earth = main heater of the air

17.s: What heats the troposphere, making it warmest near the ground?

17.s: What kind of radiation is incoming solar radiation mainly?
17.x: Sun's radiation – Short-wave: mostly visible light + short-wave (near) infra-red; about half of insolation is infra-red

17.s: What kind of radiation does the Earth give off?
17.x: Earth's radiation – Long-wave infra-red (not ultraviolet)

17.s: Which gases mainly absorb long-wave terrestrial radiation in the lower atmosphere?
17.x: Absorbers – Long-wave terrestrial radiation is absorbed mainly by carbon dioxide and water vapour (concentrated in the lower atmosphere)

17.x: Infra-red – Not part of the visible spectrum

17.s: Which of these is a short-wave process, not a way long-wave heat warms the air?

17.s: Which mode of heat transfer needs no medium?
17.x: Medium – Radiation needs no medium; conduction and convection need matter

100.s: Who gave the least-cost theory of industrial location?
